story: Guatemala's 36-year civil war killed some 200,000 people, most of them Indigenous Maya, before peace accords in 1996, whose 30th anniversary falls this year. A UN-backed anti-corruption commission, CICIG, later jailed a sitting president, until the elite it targeted had it expelled in 2019. In 2023 voters elected Bernardo Arévalo, an anti-corruption sociologist and son of the country's first democratic president. The attorney general, Consuelo Porras, then spent months trying to stop him taking office and the next two years prosecuting his party and allies.

Guatemala's president cannot fire the attorney general, so Arévalo waited. In 2026 the wait ended. Porras, sanctioned by 40 countries for obstructing anti-corruption work, was left off the shortlist for another term, and on 5 May Arévalo named lawyer Gabriel García Luna to replace her when her term ended on 17 May (AP via WTOP). "The Public Ministry is getting a new authority who does not come to serve a president," Arévalo said. Human Rights Watch noted that under Porras, convictions against cartels and organised crime fell sharply (HRW). For survivors of the war's massacres, whose cases stalled under her, her exit was "a sigh of relief" (JusticeInfo). The catch: Arévalo has barely a year left before the 2027 election and a Congress still dominated by the old parties, and he cannot run again.
briefing.power: A presidential republic. The president is directly elected for a single four-year term; the 160-seat Congress is fragmented. The attorney general is appointed for four years from a commission shortlist and cannot be removed by the president.
